Whether the original editor refuses an auto-join into a full group or creates a new group is a doc 03 fact to check; the removal holds either way.
frequency: workflow: per workflow; frequent on large missions near engine limits
removal: Make wrong input impossible first, then explain. The placement ghost and drag preview show the outcome before the click, using the same limit and reference functions admission uses: the auto-join target, 'group 12/12', the radio slot's owner. If a gesture is still refused, a toast at the cursor gives the finding, the owner and a one-click fix. Test: every Rejection returned to a Ui command source is rendered; none is dropped.
change_in: ui-shell §3, §6; commands-undo-history §4.1; plotroom-view, plotroom-ui

title: Undoable edits can still carry confirmation prompts
description: The command registry types Destructiveness::Destructive { confirm: ConfirmKind }, but no rule ties a confirmation to whether the command can be undone, although every document command is undoable. Designed prompts that add little: safe delete asks 'N references will break' before deleting, even though the dangling references then become diagnostics with retarget, remove and restore fixes. Dragging one sampled key of a cutscene template 'asks once to bake', although baking is undoable (doc 32 §5.1, doc 39 §7). Each prompt is an extra click, and habitual OK-clicking trains users to ignore the prompts that matter (overwriting files, exporting, launching the game). Measure: confirmations per session.
evidence: commands-undo-history §3 (CommandEffect, Destructiveness), §6-§8; core-document-model §7.3 (safe delete; a dangling reference becomes a diagnostic with fixes); doc 32 §5.1 ('asks once to bake'); doc 39 §7 step 6.
frequency: workflow: per workflow (deletes, template nudges)
removal: Eliminate the step, with a rule enforced by the type: make Destructiveness::Destructive impossible for WriteDocumentUndoable commands, with a registry test that no undoable command has a ConfirmKind. Confirmation exists only for effects outside undo: disk overwrite, export, game launch, egress. Delete runs at once with a non-blocking 'N references now dangle: Undo · Show' notice built from the existing diagnostics, and a bake happens on the drag with an 'Undo bake' toast. This governs command-level confirmations only: D024's autonomy waits on agent or workflow batches that delete, move or exceed the size threshold are separate and stay unchanged.
change_in: commands-undo-history §3; core-document-model §7.3; doc 32 §5.1 and doc 39 §7 (fold via DG035); plotroom-commands registry test

title: After any hand edit of a module's output, every parameter change asks for a three-way merge
area: editing: no-code modules (doc 31); generated regions; cutscenes and atmosphere cards
description: Walkthrough (doc 31 AT3): edit one line of a module's generated SQS, or move one of its emitted triggers, then later change the module's delay. The region is now Customized, so regeneration 'offers a three-way merge or keep-and-detach'. That is a decision card in merge jargon for a hobbyist who changed one number, and it repeats on every later parameter change. The kernel already merges fields (merge_regenerated), but text regions and emitted entities get the prompt even when the hand edit and the regenerated change do not overlap. Measure: merge prompts per 100 parameter edits on customised elements.
evidence: core-document-model §8.1 (merge_regenerated), §8.3 (RegionState; 'Customized offers a three-way merge or keep-and-detach'); doc 31 §8.3, AT3; doc 32 §6; doc 41 §3.1; doc 25 E9 (zero clobbers).
frequency: workflow: each parameter change on a customised module, sequence or atmosphere card
removal: Automate. When hunks or entities do not overlap, apply the line- and entity-level three-way merge automatically as one undo group with a 'merged around your edits: review' chip. Then re-run lowering checks and Teller on the merged output, because two non-overlapping text hunks can still merge into broken script. If the merged result fails a check, or any hunk overlaps, fall back to the side-by-side conflict view with 'keep mine' preselected. Customized regions are never overwritten silently, so zero clobbers still holds.
change_in: core-document-model §8.3; doc 31 §8.3 (fold); plotroom-doc merge; plotroom-lower

title: Advisory findings are numerous, collide in code, and come back after unrelated edits
area: editing: validation and lints; Problems panel; acknowledgements
description: About 250 provisional codes wait in the C, CF, MC, SL, AU, AL, DR, TP, VY, VX and D9-D12 families plus doc 32's cinematics lints, and most are advisory. An 'intentional' acknowledgement stays valid only while the fingerprint of every field the rule reads matches. Nudging a unit or retiming a cue therefore brings back a finding the user already dismissed. Short codes collide across docs (C6/C06, E7-E12, D9), so the same code can mean different things in the Problems panel and in a model's repair turn. Doc 41 §6 keeps info findings in a quiet list, but the architecture's Problems panel has no such rule. AU04 fires both on assignment and again at export by design, because export is the redistribution point. Measure: re-raised acknowledgements and advisory items shown per mission.
evidence: validation-and-lints §3, §5, §7 (fingerprint of the fields the rule reads), §11, §14 OQ3; docs/README §2.2 (code collisions); doc 41 §6 (quiet list) and AU04 (fires again at export); doc 32 §3.7; doc 39 §6; DG005 (open); game-integration §11 (export-scan confirmation list).
frequency: session: every session once a mission grows
removal: Safe default plus automation. (a) Fold Advisory and Info into a counted quiet list across the whole architecture, making doc 41's rule architecture-wide; Problems shows EngineError, ProfileError and Warning by default. (b) Fingerprint an 'intentional' acknowledgement over the facts that make the finding true: DiagData plus the rule's declared key inputs, decided per rule kind (validation §14 OQ3), so it survives unrelated edits. (c) Keep AU04's deliberate re-fire at export, which is a licence warning at the moment of sharing, but fold export-time repeats into the single export-scan confirmation list (game-integration §11), so they appear once there rather than as new Problems entries. (d) Users and models see only canonical registry ids (DG005).
change_in: validation-and-lints §7, §11, §14 OQ3; ui-shell §6 (Problems row); DG005; doc 41 §6 (fold); game-integration §11

title: Binarized and packed missions: a read-only dead end in one design, implicit conversion in another
area: editing: import and preserve of existing missions
description: Walkthrough: a user opens a downloaded mission whose mission.sqm is binarized (raP), which is common for released missions, to fix one trigger. The core model opens raP read-only and requires an explicit 'Convert to text' command (guarantee R10). The first edit attempt fails, and the user has to find the command. Doc 37's power-tools table says a PBO or a binarized mission opens and 'saving writes text into the project'. Users hit a mode wall, and contributors get two contradictory specifications.
evidence: core-document-model §2 (raP opens read-only), §12 R10; doc 37 power-tools table, row 'Open packed missions' (WA15); doc 09 P10, S12; roadmap M1 goal ('open any mission, from a folder or a PBO').
frequency: workflow: every binarized or packed mission opened for editing
removal: Eliminate the step, with a visible default. The first edit gesture on a raP document performs 'Convert to text' and the edit as one undo group, announced by an inline banner ('binarized: this edit converts it to text; the original is kept as .bak'). A PBO always opens as a new unpacked project folder and is never edited in place. R10's intent stays: conversion is a recorded, announced, undoable command, never silent. File a DG, since two docs disagree and R10's wording changes.
change_in: core-document-model §2, §12 R10; doc 37 §7 (fold); new DG

title: Round trips through the stock editor, and first imports, ask about each element separately
area: editing: import and preserve; identity re-matching; lift recognisers
description: Users who alternate with the game's own editor, which renumbers ids on every save, reopen the mission in Plotroom and go through re-matching. Each Ambiguous match is 'asked about, never guessed', one question per element, and each unmatched item gets its own 'identity re-assigned' diagnostic. On first open of an older mission, each of about 25 idiom recognisers can offer a lift with evidence and a diff. The designs say how each offer looks, not how many can arrive at once. Measure: questions per reopen after a stock-editor save, and lift offers per import, on the opt-in corpus.
evidence: core-document-model §7.2 (Rematch; thresholds [U], doc 45 OQ9); doc 31 §8.1-§8.2 ('offer, never force'); doc 37 TL;DR (about 25 recognisers); doc 19 §7.6.
frequency: workflow: per external save; per first import
removal: Automate by batching. One review card per reopen ('14 matched, 2 need a look') with 'accept all confident'; Ambiguous matches are excluded from that button and stay individually confirmed with the best candidate preselected, never guessed. Unmatched-id notices are grouped into one diagnostic. Lift offers are collected into one quiet 'N patterns could become modules' chip, reviewed as a list, and never interrupt the open. Thresholds are measured on the corpus first, as §7.2 already plans. Batching changes only how questions are presented.
change_in: core-document-model §7.2; doc 31 §8.2 (fold); ui-shell §6 (a review surface)

title: Target profile: two different defaults in the docs, no preview before a switch, no rule for a campaign and its missions
description: D003 makes Cwr the default profile. Doc 19 §3 principle 5 says 'the Cwa199 target is the default' for the campaign designer, so a contributor following doc 19 builds a different default. Switching a mission to Cwa199 greys out Cwr/Ce features (doc 31 AT11) and turns existing content into ProfileErrors all at once. A 'retarget' preview is only an open question (validation §14 OQ4). A campaign and each of its missions carry their own profile, and no doc says whether a mission inherits the campaign's profile or what happens when the two differ.
evidence: D003 decision 3; doc 19 §3 item 5; validation-and-lints §8, §14 OQ4; doc 31 AT11; core-document-model §10 (project.toml per mission and per campaign folder).
frequency: workflow: every new mission or campaign, every profile change
removal: Safe default plus a preview. Fold doc 19 to D003 (Cwr), or to whatever D003 says after the amendment proposed in FR-P-004. A mission created inside a campaign inherits the campaign's profile, and a mismatch is a Warning with an 'align' fix. The profile picker shows a dry run of the switch before applying it (new ProfileErrors, features that will lower differently), then applies it as one undo group.
change_in: doc 19 §3 (fold); validation-and-lints §8, §14 OQ4; core-document-model §10; plotroom-profile
effort: S doc fold; M dry run

title: Two expression languages can land in the same field
area: editing: rule builder; campaign designer; trigger and presence conditions
description: Engine fields (trigger condition, On Activation, presence condition) hold SQS; rules and campaign guards use CXL. Doc 19 §6.6 says trigger and presence conditions 'accept CXL' and lowers it into expCond and presenceCondition. The two languages differ exactly where people and models slip: CXL has a boolean '==' and typed enums; SQS has no boolean '==' and compares strings case-insensitively (doc 19 F1, F3). The same text can be valid in one and wrong in the other, and nothing in the design tells the user or the model which language a field expects. DG008 unifies the CXL scopes but does not address CXL and SQS sharing one field.
evidence: doc 19 §5, F1, F3, §6.6; doc 31 §5.1, §5.3 item 6; DG008 (open); validation-and-lints §9 (check modes per field); core-document-model §3.3 (FieldDescriptor.check), §8.3 (mission.sqm field provenance is sidecar-only).
frequency: workflow: every condition written in a campaign-managed mission
removal: Make wrong input impossible. Each expression field has exactly one language, shown as a chip (CXL or SQS). CXL lives in the rule and condition builder and in a separate 'campaign condition' slot. Its lowering is combined with the raw SQS field as (lowered CXL) && (user SQS) and tracked as a sidecar owned region, because mission.sqm field provenance is sidecar-only (core §8.3), not a text fence inside the field. The raw engine field stays SQS. Conversion between languages is an explicit, previewed command, and model tool schemas state each field's language.
change_in: doc 19 §6.6 (fold); DG008 (add a field-language rule); core-document-model §3.3 descriptor check modes

title: Several words for one concept, and one word for several (including five meanings of 'Classic')
description: Turning generated content into plain content has five names: 'Detach to script' (doc 31 N1), 'Eject' (doc 31 §8.3, core §8.3), the region state 'Detached', 'keep-and-detach' in merges, and template 'Detach' (core §8.2), which means something else. 'Classic' names the classic renderer and view, the Classic dock layout, the Classic keymap, the fallback look-alike theme, the Classic campaign complexity tier and the music plan 'QP1 Classic OFP', and doc 34 le16 adds an 'OFP 2001 Classic' feel preset; nothing states which dock layout (Workbench or Classic) a first run opens with. At least four dials control disclosure: Easy/Advanced (D029), campaign complexity tiers (doc 19 §6.8), the realism level (validation §3) and module 'Advanced' folds (doc 31 §4.1), plus Standing Orders density. Coined names (Plotline, the Tote, Teller, Wilco, Standing Orders, Drill) label panels without saying what they do. Newcomers and models have to learn the mapping, and tool descriptions inherit the ambiguity. Merged from a duplicate first-run finding about 'Classic'.
evidence: doc 31 N1, §4.1, §8.3; core-document-model §8.2-§8.3; ui-shell §2-§3 (classic renderer and view), §6 (Workbench and Classic layouts; Plotline; the Tote), §8 (Classic keymap), §12; doc 05 §7.4 ('Classic look-alike' theme); doc 34 le16; doc 19 §6.8; doc 41 §5.2 QP1; validation-and-lints §3; D029; D002; D034; DG037.
frequency: session: every session
removal: Explain at the point of friction, since the product names are owner-decided (D002, D034). The DG037 names table gets one verb per concept (for example, Eject means 'turn into plain content', and Detach is reserved for templates). 'Classic' is reserved for the faithful look; a single feel preset chosen once (a '2001 editor feel' that bundles look, layout and keymap, le16) replaces the scattered meanings, and ui-shell states the first-run default layout. Disclosure is presented as one 'show more' system with Easy/Advanced as its preset, which is D029's own framing. Panel titles pair the product name with its function ('The Tote: campaign state'). Command ids and tool descriptions use the same words. Resolve in one names-table pass with FR-C-009 and FR-P-076.
change_in: DG037 names table; D034; core-document-model §8.3; doc 31 (fold); ui-shell §6, §8, §12

title: Campaign state setup the editor could do itself: declare-before-use and untyped imported variables
area: editing: campaign designer (Plotline, the Tote); campaign import
description: Only declared variables exist, so a guard that mentions a new flag is error C06 until the user leaves the builder, declares the variable in the Tote and comes back. On import, the saveVar names found in scripts become Opaque variables. They must be typed by hand before a retrofit router can read them, although the importer already saw their assignments. Measure: C06 findings resolved by declaring a variable, and Opaque variables left untyped after import.
evidence: doc 19 §3 item 2, §4, §6.5 (C06), §7.6 items 3 and 5; ui-shell §6 (the Tote).
frequency: workflow: branching campaigns; imports
removal: Automate without weakening declarations. An unknown name in a guard offers one click: 'Declare x as Bool in campaign scope', with type and scope inferred from the use. Opaque variables arrive with a type proposed from their observed literal assignments (Bool, a bounded Int range, an Enum from string literals) as a prefilled chip the user confirms. A declaration remains an explicit, typed, undoable command.
change_in: doc 19 §4, §7.6 (fold); plotroom-cxl quick fixes; plotroom-campaign import

title: Mode errors in the F1-F6 map modes
description: What a double-click creates depends on the active mode (units, groups, triggers, waypoints, synchronisation, markers). In the wrong mode it creates the wrong kind of object, or nothing. The faithful behaviour stays (D004), but newcomers learned it by trial (doc 09 P8), and F1 cannot be the help key because it is Units mode. Measure: an insert undone within a few seconds and followed by a mode change.
evidence: ui-shell §3, §6 (Standing Orders row, F1), §8; D004 item 1; doc 09 P8; doc 34 le06; commands-undo-history §10 (ViewState.mode).
frequency: session: every session for newcomers
removal: Explain at the point, and remove a step without changing the modes. The cursor shows the active mode and what a double-click will create. Palette actions ('place trigger here') and a right-click 'insert ... here' switch the mode as part of the action. Undo restores the previous mode along with removing the object; the map mode is view state, so this can use the same mechanism as selection_before and selection_after in UndoGroup. Resolve together with FR-P-016.
change_in: ui-shell §3, §8; plotroom-view

title: Finding out why a rule or module did not fire needs a Preview run
description: Rule debugging (the fire log, 'why didn't this fire?', 'Try it') runs through the game harness on Cwr/Ce and waits for DG001's non-aborting launch. On Cwa199 only a debug export with hint tracepoints exists. Many 'why not' answers are static and computable in the editor: a guard reads a flag nobody sets; the chain goes through a disabled rule; a radio item is hidden because the player does not lead the group (doc 19 F11); a condition is not Bool, so it is silently false (doc 31 §5.3 item 6); trigger latency is up to 0.5 s.
evidence: doc 31 §5.3-§5.5, §7.4, §7.5; DG001 (open); doc 19 F11; core-document-model §9 (the CXL engine-faithful evaluator).
frequency: workflow: every rule-debugging session
removal: Automate. A static 'Can this fire?' explainer built on the CXL evaluator and the flag graph lists the setters of every flag the rule reads, setters that can never run, and engine preconditions (leader-only radio, 0.5 s latency, Bool check), each linked on the map. The live fire log stays for runtime facts. Nothing is launched and nothing waits on DG001.
change_in: doc 31 §5.4 (fold); plotroom-modules rule analysis; validation-and-lints §10

title: v1 camera work is hand-written script, although its cheapest tools need no live link
description: D036 ships the Cutscene-node recipe and 'camera scripting through the script editor' in v1; the timeline and the director come in v1.2. A v1 user making an intro is back to the classic workflow: fly the in-game camera, find clipboard.txt, paste blocks, fix quoted debug-name targets, and remember the safe epilogue. Doc 32 already designs parts that need neither the timeline nor the harness: tailing clipboard.txt, 'insert capture' at the cursor, the live map reading of hand-written camera scripts (path and FOV wedges), and the camera lints (unbalanced input lock, a title-layer BLACK OUT before an END, terminate before camDestroy). Capture blocks appear in 32 of 34 official intros. game-integration §7 currently places clipboard capture in v1.x. Measure: steps and minutes for doc 32's AT6 intro in v1.
evidence: D036 item 5; D015 amendment note; doc 32 §3.7, §3.8 ('Scripters keep the tools'), §4.4; doc 39 §9.1 (Capture row); doc 31 §7.2 (camera lints); game-integration §7 (clipboard capture in v1.x).
frequency: workflow: every intro, outro or cutscene made in v1
removal: Automate. Bring into v1's script editor (Teller): clipboard tailing with 'insert capture', the read-only map reading of camera scripts, the doc 32 §3.7 error lints, and a one-click 'wrap in safe epilogue' fix. None of these depends on the timeline or the harness. Reading the game's clipboard output is a product read of the user's game data, not agent file access. Moving capture into v1 is a roadmap or owner scope change.
change_in: D036 item 5 (owner) or roadmap M4 scope; game-integration §7; doc 32 §7 phase plan; plotroom-teller

title: Undo history ends at restart without saying so
description: History is session-only by design (the type is not Serialize). After closing and reopening, undo is empty and nothing marks the boundary. The crash op journal holds the same op batches but is used only after a crash. Users coming from the original editor (no undo at all, doc 09 P1) may accept this; users of modern editors will reach for undo after reopening and get nothing.
evidence: commands-undo-history §8 (Hygiene; an 'older history trimmed' row already exists); core-document-model §11 (crash op journal, .bak); roadmap M2 (autosave and rotating backups); doc 09 P1.
frequency: session: at each session boundary
removal: Explain at the point of friction. The History panel's first row reads 'Opened at 14:02; earlier changes: compare with a backup...' and links the rotating backups with a semantic diff. Undo at that boundary shows the same message instead of doing nothing. History stays session-only.
change_in: commands-undo-history §8; ui-shell §6 (History row)

title: A small hand edit silently takes ownership of a field and later blocks regeneration
area: editing: provenance; partial regeneration; glass box
description: Any User-origin SetField on a generated element makes that field human-owned automatically, which is the right rule. It also happens on accidental nudges. Later, 'regenerate' or a workflow re-run keeps those fields, and the user wonders why the change did not apply. The reason is shown only in the inspector's value-source badge, not in the regeneration result.
evidence: core-document-model §8.1 (automatic human ownership), §8.3; ui-shell §5 (value-source badges), §7; doc 39 §7 (pinned shots keep their keys); doc 25 §9.
frequency: workflow: every partial regeneration
removal: Explain at the point of friction. The regeneration result says 'kept 3 fields you edited' and lists each field with its current value, the regenerated value, and a per-field 'use the new value' button, which carries UserIntent. The ownership rules and the no-clobber invariant do not change.
change_in: core-document-model §8.1; doc 25 §9 (fold); ui-shell §7

title: Scripters who keep their own text editor lose Teller
description: Many community scripters work in external editors (doc 09 P3; doc 31 lists Chris' Script Editor among the most-downloaded tools). Teller is embedded in Plotroom's script panel, and an LSP binary is 'optional and later'. The file watcher notices external changes, but the design does not say that diagnostics refresh from them.
evidence: validation-and-lints §9 ('an LSP binary is optional and later'), §13; core-document-model §11 (file watcher; reload / overwrite / diff choice); doc 09 P3; doc 31 TL;DR; D036 item 3 (plotroom check CLI).
frequency: session: every session for scripters who use an external editor
removal: Automate. An external save of a clean buffer is reloaded through the existing external-change path and re-linted at once, highlighting its Problems entries with the same mission-aware checks the panel uses; when Plotroom has unsaved edits to the same file, the reload / overwrite / diff choice of core §11 applies. 'plotroom check --file' gives the same diagnostics for editor tasks. Record Teller's stdio LSP mode as a post-v1 item with its scope.
change_in: validation-and-lints §9, §13; core-document-model §11; plotroom-cli

title: Edit tool names follow four different conventions
description: CommandSpec ids are 'area.object.verb' (mission.waypoint.add), and a ProposeOp names a CommandId. The research docs hand models other shapes: module.propose(def, params), rule.propose(slots), campaign.add_node, connect(...), campaign.declare_var, campaign.propose_branch, cine.fill, screenplay.write, atmo.apply, audio.plan_cues, script.fix(diagnostic_id). Verb position, dots versus snake_case, and propose versus apply wording differ by doc. Inconsistent names raise wrong-call and ToolNotInStep rates for small models, and contributors have to guess which list is canonical. Measure: wrong-tool and ToolNotInStep rates per step kind.
evidence: commands-undo-history §3 (id scheme; one registry generates Wilco and MCP tools; schemas from /// docs), §12 OQ6; agent-runtime §2 (ProposeOp), §8 ('names provisional'); doc 19 §8; doc 31 §9; doc 32 §5.3; doc 39 §8; doc 41 §7.
frequency: constant: every model call that edits
removal: Make wrong input impossible. Tool names exist only as generated CommandSpec ids that follow one grammar; research docs refer to them by id in their next fold. A registry test rejects ids outside the grammar and near-duplicate verbs for the same effect (propose, apply, fill). Fits DG032. Resolve together with FR-M-018.
change_in: commands-undo-history §3, §12 OQ6; docs 19, 31, 32, 39, 41 (fold); plotroom-commands registry test

title: campaign.connect asks the model for CXL text and an integer rank
description: Doc 19 §8's connect(from, on, guard_cxl, effects_cxl, to, rank) makes any model write guard and effect text and choose a rank number. Doc 31 §9 limits free CXL to strong, qualified models, and doc 63 puts Compose at FR5 (a freedom level, not a register id). A weak model that writes 'camp.bridge == true' or a colliding rank gets a rejection and a repair turn that typed slots would have avoided. The rank also depends on the table's current order, which the model may not have in its context. Measure: repair turns per connect call, per model tier.
evidence: doc 19 §5.5, §6.2 (rank u16, drag to reorder), §8; doc 31 §9; doc 63 §2 (freedom levels); doc 25 §7.2; DG008; D009 (code computes valid options).
frequency: workflow: every campaign branch built by Wilco or an external agent
removal: Make wrong input impossible. Below freedom level FR5 the tool takes a guard as typed atoms (a variable picked from the declared list, a comparator allowed by its type, a value from its domain) and a position as 'before or after edge X' or 'last'. Code prints the CXL and computes ranks. CXL text stays available at FR5 and above, behind the same checker.
change_in: doc 19 §8 (fold); DG008; agent-runtime §6; plotroom-campaign commands

title: Element references handed to models are long 128-bit ids
area: editing: model-facing edit tools; token economy
description: An ItemRef is displayed as a typed prefix plus a 128-bit time-ordered id (unit_..., grp_..., wp_...). Every Build-mode proposal, MCP call and repair turn copies these ids. They cost tokens on every mention, and small models mistype them, which surfaces as dangling-reference rejections. Doc 61 proposes opaque, revision-bound handles, but only for Teller results. Measure: tokens per referenced element, and rejections caused by mistyped ids.
evidence: core-document-model §7.1; agent-runtime §2, §9; doc 61 TL;DR (handles); D026; doc 57 (capsules).
frequency: constant: every model call that references mission or campaign elements
removal: Make wrong input impossible and cut tokens. Model-facing surfaces use short per-capsule handles (u1, g3) that the harness maps to ElementRefs and binds to the snapshot revision. An unknown or stale handle is rejected with the current list. For the glass box, the decision journal records the handle-to-ElementRef map per capsule, so the inspector and replay show real references. Full ids stay in journals, the sidecar, and external APIs that ask for them.
change_in: agent-runtime §2, §6; doc 61 §4 (extend handles to every element reference); plotroom-wilco

title: Research designs still show pre-rename names, and generated identifiers are missing from the rename table
area: editing: design docs for modules, campaigns and cinematics
description: Doc 31 sketches 'ofp-modules', ModuleInstanceId(u32), 'pinned: bool' and generated files under 'ofpe\'. Doc 19 uses 'ofp-campaign-*' crates, NodeId(u32) and 'ofp-editor.campaign.toml'. Doc 32's example emits '; ofp-editor:generated' headers, 'ofpe_cam' and 'ofpe_seq_...' globals, and 'ofpe_a_<n>' unit names in mission.sqm ('ofpe_' occurs 26 times in doc 32 and 5 times in doc 39). crate-map §15 maps crates, folders, headers and module keys. It does not cover generated global-variable prefixes or generated object names. An agent implementing a lowering will therefore copy 'ofpe_' into every mission, which is the kind of third-party mark AGENTS.md keeps out of generated content.
evidence: crate-map §15; core-document-model §7.1, §8.1 (Pin enum), §8.3; doc 31 §4.2, §4.4; doc 19 §4.2, §7.1, §9; doc 32 §3.5; AGENTS.md 'Naming and Trademarks'; testing-strategy §14 (hygiene grep).
frequency: workflow: every implementation session in these areas
removal: Automate, with a safe default. Add the generated-identifier prefix (globals, object names, sequence ids) to the §15 table. Extend the CI hygiene grep to template packs and golden lowering outputs. Until docs 19, 31, 32 and 39 are folded, put a one-line 'names superseded, see crate-map §15' banner at the top of each.
change_in: crate-map §15; testing-strategy §14; docs 19, 31, 32, 39 (banner, then fold)

title: The editing core is gated on seven open technical design gaps
area: editing: attributes, modules, rules, conditions, cinematics, codes
description: Seven technical DGs are open (all 'decision by: technical'): DG003 (attribute vocabulary), DG004 (what a module is), DG005 (code registry, also an M1 gate), DG007 (one definition format), DG008 (condition language), DG009 (owner of the cinematic engine facts) and DG035 (the director's changes to sibling docs). Each blocks a crate: plotroom-modules, plotroom-cxl, plotroom-cine, plotroom-diag. Dependent work stays proposal-only until they close, although most already carry a recommended resolution.
evidence: design-gap-requests README (rows DG003-DG009, DG035; each decision must cite the evidence its request names); docs/README §3.2 item 5; D015 open parts; roadmap M1 gates (DG005).
frequency: workflow: per implementation milestone (M1-M4)
removal: Safe default. Schedule a design round that adopts each technical DG's recommended resolution unless someone records an objection by a set date, and close them in one change set before the milestone that needs them, DG005 first because it is an M1 gate. Adopting by default at a deadline is a scheduling device only: each decision still cites the evidence its request names. The DG index shows which milestone each DG blocks.
change_in: design-gap-requests README; DG003, DG004, DG005, DG007, DG008, DG009, DG035; roadmap milestone gates

title: Adding one lint means hand-writing a registry row, a data file and two fixtures, in a code space not yet assigned
area: editing: validation and lints; code registry
description: Codes are data. Each needs a registry row, a data file (summary, why it matters, fix hint, profiles, suppressibility), a failing and a passing fixture, and xtask regeneration of the DiagCode enum. That is good for quality but heavy per rule. About 250 provisional codes wait in more than 12 families, several of which collide, and no field says which milestone needs which code. Until DG005 lands, contributors can use provisional ids but have no final ids. Measure: files touched and minutes per new rule.
evidence: validation-and-lints §5, §10; docs/README §2.2 (collisions); DG005 (open; its table lists the collisions; option C, canonical dotted slugs); roadmap M1 gate; testing-strategy.
frequency: workflow: every rule added
removal: Automate. 'xtask new-rule <family> <kind>' writes the data file with the required fields marked TODO, and generates failing and passing fixture skeletons with the testkit builders plus the test stub. To avoid id collisions between branches, the author chooses the canonical dotted slug (DG005 option C), the short code is assigned at merge, and the CI duplicate check rejects clashes. The generated data file and fixture skeletons fail CI while any TODO field or placeholder fixture remains, so the scaffold cannot ship an unchecked rule. The registry gains a milestone column, so v1 carries only the codes it uses.
change_in: validation-and-lints §5; DG005; xtask; plotroom-diag

title: The v1 Cutscene-node recipe has no single specification
description: v1 ships only the Cutscene-node recipe (D036 item 5). Its content is spread over at least seven places: doc 32 (model and compiler, written for the full timeline); doc 39 §1.2's requested changes (DG035, open), such as the eye-height rules and gates; doc 35 rc35/rc50 timing defaults, which core §9 calls 'provisional until reconciled with doc 39 §9.4 through DG035' (doc 39 has no §9.4; its reconciliation with doc 35 is §9.3, and roadmap integration-owners I35-CUT repeats the same pointer); doc 19, which defines the Cutscene node (DG035 rows 3 and 9 say it takes the rc35 band); validation-and-lints §10 (MC25, MC26 ship in v1 with the node); the one-line Cinematics row in core §9; and D036 itself. An implementer has to merge all of them and guess which v1.2 parts to leave out.
evidence: D036 item 5; core-document-model §9 (Cinematics row); crate-map (plotroom-cine row); ui-shell §6 (Cinematics row); doc 32 §3; doc 39 §1.2, §9.3; doc 19 (Cutscene node); validation-and-lints §10 (MC25, MC26); DG035; DG009.
frequency: once: per implementation (the milestone that lands plotroom-cine)
removal: Eliminate the step. Fold DG035 first, then write one architecture subsection for the v1 Cutscene-node recipe from D036 item 5, core §9, doc 32 §3, doc 35 rc35/rc50, doc 39 §1.2/§9.3, doc 19's Cutscene node and validation-and-lints §10's MC25/MC26. It states fields, hosts, lints, defaults and what is deferred to v1.2. crate-map's plotroom-cine row and ui-shell's Cinematics row then point to it.
change_in: core-document-model §9 or a new architecture section; doc 32 (fold); DG035; crate-map; ui-shell §6

title: Plan card gates every writing run, even a one-step, free, undoable edit
description: Under the default Confirm autonomy, every workflow that can write opens a plan card, and nothing happens until it is clicked (doc 38 §5.4: 'Once per run'). Every chat request is dispatched into a workflow, so a request like 'give this group a patrol' costs an extra click on a card that adds no information: the effect is one undoable group, the run costs nothing when AI is off or the model is local, and nothing is deleted. Doc 21 §4.2 and §7.3 describe the same case the opposite way ('lands as one undo group, so a misreading costs one undo'), so the design also contradicts itself. The escape hatch, 'Always run without the card in this project', is set per workflow and per project, and users find it only after they have hit the friction. Measure: one extra click and one card to read per small AI edit, so 20 small requests in a session mean 20 cards.
evidence: D024 item 2, Confirm row ('An edit the user asked for lands as one highlighted undo group; plans are approved once'); doc 38 §5.2 ('Before a run that can write, a non-modal card'), §5.4 Confirm row ('Once per run'); doc 21 §4.2 ('Show the reading ... lands as one undo group') and §7.3 ('Undoable edits need no dialog because a misreading costs one undo'); agent-runtime §9 (free text goes through IntentFill and Dispatch into a workflow).
frequency: constant: every small AI edit
removal: Eliminate the step. Under Confirm, skip the card and show it afterwards as a receipt (the workflow, the reading 'read ... as Populate area', the setup used, plus Undo) only when all of these hold: every effect is an undoable create or set; no write touches a human-owned or pinned field (those need UserIntent anyway); there is no plugin egress, no Preview offer that auto-launches and no delete or move of existing entities; the run has no ask or approve step; the cost is $0 or within the per-run cap already set; the origin is not an external agent; and the written set fits the size threshold (see FR-P-062). In every other case the card stays. Undo, validation and provenance are unchanged. The rule is defined once, in the wait-policy table (FR-C-008); the D024 Confirm row wording is an owner decision. Resolve together with FR-P-033.
change_in: D024 (Confirm row wording); doc 38 §5.2, §5.4; doc 21 §4.2, §7.3; agent-runtime §11; plotroom-workflow-runtime admission
effort: S for the doc rule; M for the runtime predicate and its tests

title: The plan card carries about 17 groups of information before Run
description: Six documents each add fields to the plan card: per step the kind icon, title, role, bound model setup, K and R; declared effects and required plugins; estimated turns, time and cost, with the price date and the cap; two or three cheaper alternatives and the $0 path; per-provider quota lines with reset times and host health, and 'fits today'; three buttons for when every route is busy, and an auto-resume checkbox; assumption chips and the check-ins choice; the 'asked as' level, with the 'bigger step' and 'smaller steps' offers; Run, Edit, Cancel and 'always run without the card'. Most of this does not help the one decision the card asks for: run this or not. Users either skim it, and then the card informs nobody, or they stall.
evidence: doc 38 §5.2; doc 40 §6 (example card); doc 52 §5.4 (example plan card with quota lines, busy choices and auto-resume); D024 item 3 (check-ins); doc 63 TL;DR and §7 ('asked as' on the plan card, 'Bigger step' offer, 'Smaller steps' toggle); ui-shell §6, row 'Plan card and run panel'. Measure: about 17 groups of information before Run; the target is 3 lines above the fold.
frequency: constant: every plan card
removal: Explain at the point of friction, once the safe defaults are in place. The card leads with three code-written lines and Run: (1) what the run will do: scope and effect, for example 'adds 8 missions, deletes nothing'; (2) what it costs and how long it takes: one number, with the $0 alternative shown only when the cost is above zero; (3) when it will stop for you (the stop timeline of FR-P-068). Steps, roles, K and R, quota lines, route lists and 'asked as' levels move under Details. Details opens by default only when a warning applies: an unassigned role, a run over its cap, a run that does not fit today, or egress. Layered disclosure removes nothing, so the glass box holds. Measure time-to-Run and how often users open Details.
change_in: doc 38 §5.2; doc 40 §6; doc 52 §5.4; doc 63 §7; ui-shell §6

title: The size threshold can ask again for batches inside a plan the user already approved
description: Under Confirm, batches that 'exceed a size threshold wait for one click'. The threshold is not set, and nothing says whether it applies to create-only batches inside a plan the user already approved. In campaign-from-brief, S6 builds every node deterministically after the outline is approved. If each node's commit trips the threshold, an 8-mission campaign asks 8 more times about content the user just approved as a whole. Doc 63 also counts on this threshold to catch larger steps, so a more capable model that is granted bigger steps produces more clicks. That works against the capability ladder's own aim.
evidence: D024 item 2 (Confirm row); doc 21 §7.3 and OQ3 ('Which ... Confirm size threshold avoid nagging (needs alpha data)'); doc 38 §5.4 (Confirm row, approve column); agent-runtime §9 (every chat request is dispatched into a workflow), §10 (S3 approve then commit; S6 builds each node); doc 63 §7 ('larger batches already trip Confirm's delete, move or size threshold'). Measure: up to one extra click per node after the outline is approved.
frequency: workflow: campaign and large mission runs
removal: Eliminate the step. An approved plan whose card stated its scope and write set pre-authorises create and set batches inside that scope, and size alone never triggers a wait inside an approved run. Inside an approved run, a wait is triggered only by deleting or moving pre-existing entities, writing human-owned or pinned fields, or writing outside the approved scope. Because every chat request is dispatched into a workflow, there is no separate category of 'unplanned direct chat edits': apply the size threshold to runs that skipped the card under the receipt rule (FR-P-060) and to Auto. Set its value from alpha data (doc 21 OQ3). Changing D024's Confirm row wording is an owner decision; typed undoable commands and checks are unchanged.
change_in: D024 item 2; doc 21 §7.3; doc 38 §5.4; commands-undo-history §4 (admission)

title: Four controls decide how often Wilco stops or may write, and they can contradict each other
description: Four user-visible controls govern waiting or writing: chat modes (Ask, Build, Teach, Review), each with a fixed tool set; autonomy (Ask, Propose, Confirm, Auto); the per-run check-ins choice (end only; premise and outline; every stage); and 'Always run without the card', set per workflow. Some combinations have no specified behaviour, such as Build chat mode with Ask autonomy, or Ask chat mode with Auto autonomy [I]. 'Ask' is a level of both controls. On the model side, Dispatch can resolve an edit request to a workflow that the current chat mode's tool set cannot run. Auto must also be switched on again every session. Measure: 4 x 4 x 3 = 48 combinations of three controls, before the per-workflow switch.
evidence: agent-runtime §9 (chat modes with fixed tool sets; DG023 option B, a proposal) and §11; D024 items 2-3; doc 38 §5.2 ('Always run without the card') and §5.4 Ask row ('switch to Propose'); D024 table, Auto row ('Opt-in per session'); roadmap M4 ('Ask, Build, Teach and Review modes').
frequency: session: every session

Show the check-ins choice only on the plan card of runs that have ask or approve steps, as an override of autonomy's default. Keep Auto per session by default, and offer 'Auto for this project' as an explicit setting with a persistent status-bar badge (changes D024's 'Opt-in per session', so it needs the owner). title: A user's own strong cloud key gets the weakest-model treatment until it is qualified
description: Step shapes are granted by qualification records. A setup without a record runs Pick only (freedom level FR2 in doc 63), offers Fill only as a pre-fill the user confirms, and gets no Compose or Draft; TS1 gives it no lookups. Required workflows (briefing prose, dialogue, translation drafts) then fall back to the template path. Every model outside the recommended list installs as 'custom, unqualified', and no cloud setup is qualified yet. So someone who connects a capable key first sees fewer features, an extra confirm click per field, and a qualification check they must run, spending their own calls (14-29 or more consecutive passes per setup, preset, DecisionKind and level), before briefings can be written. The connect flow never tells them any of this, and the docs never say how the project would qualify and ship a grant for a paid cloud setup. Merged from a duplicate model-facing finding about strong cloud models starting at the smallest steps.
evidence: agent-runtime §7 ('A setup with no record runs Pick with cards and offers Fill only as a pre-fill the user confirms; Compose and Draft need a record'), §12 ('No cloud measurement exists yet'), §13 ('custom'; 'unqualified' badge until qualified); doc 21 §6.3 (Required examples); doc 52 §6.1, D045 bullet item 5; D045 item 4; D044 Consequences; doc 63 §4.1 ('An unqualified setup runs FR2'), §4.3 (n >= 14 and n >= 29), §4.6; doc 61 §4.10 (TS1 for every unqualified setup); doc 51 §4.8 (re-checks spend the user's quota); roadmap risk table (Fill as a confirmed pre-fill).
frequency: constant: every workflow run on an unqualified setup
removal: Automate, and choose safe defaults. (1) Before each release the project qualifies pinned paid cloud setups on synthetic suites and ships dated grants beside the [[price]] rows, as D045 already requires for free presets; a served-model mismatch (MA4) or a DG012 trigger voids them, because cloud models change behind one id. Who may issue grants for cloud setups is an owner decision under D037 and D045. (2) The connect flow states what an unqualified setup can and cannot do. (3) A staged, priced 'Check this model' grants lower levels first (freedom levels FR3-FR4 after the smallest n), so the user gains before the full run ends. (4) Per-field pre-fill confirmations within one run are batched into one review card with 'accept all', never one card per field. Shapes are still granted only by qualification. Resolve together with FR-P-021 and FR-P-080.
change_in: agent-runtime §7, §13; D037 and D045 (qualification scope; who issues cloud grants); doc 50 §4; doc 63 §4.3; DG012; plotroom-evals; models.toml
effort: M-L (the qualification runs are the main cost)

title: Six roles must be bound by hand before AI runs can use a model, and an unbound role silently takes the failure route
description: Wilco has six roles: router, writer, scripter, explainer, play-tester and translator. The user binds each one in Settings. An unbound role shows 'unassigned', and its steps do not block: they silently follow their failure route, which means template text or defaults. A newcomer who connects one model and runs a workflow therefore gets defaults without being asked, and learns why only from the run report. The plan card shows bindings, but they can be changed only in Settings, which forces a context switch in the middle of a decision. Proposals already in progress will enlarge this surface: route lists per role (doc 52 RG1), two-stage bindings (doc 53) and per-role 'largest step' caps (doc 63). Measure: 6 bindings plus one connect before the first model-assisted result.
evidence: D024 item 4; doc 21 §7.2; agent-runtime §11 ('set explicitly in Settings'); doc 38 §5.2 ('Role bindings are shown and changed only in Settings'); doc 52 §6.1 (D024 bullet; RG1); doc 53 §4 (two-stage role binding); doc 63 §7 (Settings, Roles cap).
frequency: once: until bound; affects every run that needs an unbound role
removal: Choose a safe default and automate it. When the user connects or installs a model, propose a complete binding of every role that setup is qualified for, applied with one click, listed explicitly and recorded in Settings. Roles it is not qualified for stay unassigned, with the reason shown. Before Run, the plan card flags any unassigned role a step needs ('writer unassigned: template text') and offers an inline 'bind' that edits the Settings row in place (a design edit to doc 38 §5.2's Settings-only rule). Binding stays explicit and visible, so 'no silent switch' (D023 decision 3) still holds. Resolve together with FR-P-022.
change_in: D024 item 4; doc 21 §7.2; doc 38 §5.2; agent-runtime §11, §13; doc 50 §4

title: A free setup that meets the UX standard needs three accounts, a local model and a hand-made route list
area: wilco-ux: connect a model / free setup
description: Doc 52 finds that OpenRouter's one-click preset alone is a 'taster' that misses the proposed UX standard. The recommended free setup is the user's own OpenRouter, Groq and Cloudflare accounts plus a local model. Each account goes through its own disclosure card and OAuth or token flow, and then the user writes an ordered route list. 'Check this model' on OpenRouter spends about 30 of the user's 50 free requests for the day. The user pays for heavy setup, in steps and in quota, before the first useful run. Measure: 3 disclosure cards, 3 account flows, 1 model download and route-list authoring, about 10 steps or more before the standard is met.
evidence: doc 52 §4 ('recommended free setup': OpenRouter, Groq and Cloudflare accounts and a local model; 'a taster'), §5.1 principles 2-3 (user-created accounts; route lists authored by the user), §6.1 (D045 and doc 50 bullet, item 1); doc 50 §4 steps 0-9 (step 9: '30 of your 50 free requests today'); D045 items 1, 3 and 4; doc 21 §12.3 (smoke check); D050 item 2 and its Friction consequence (recorded after this row) make two free providers plus a local model the recommended free setup.
frequency: once: one-time setup, repeated on every provider change
removal: Automate and eliminate steps. One guided 'set up free AI' checklist chains the connects in order, shows progress and says what each adds ('with Groq: campaign text fits in a day'); account creation stays with the user (doc 52 §5.1 item 2). The checklist generates the route list from the connected, qualified entries, for one-click acceptance; the list stays visible and editable (RG1: adopted by D050 item 3 on 2026-09-28). Offered presets ship with dated qualification (D045 item 4), so 'Check this model' is not offered for them. For custom entries, run the six-call smoke check first, and the full suite only on request, with its quota cost shown. Scope and egress rules are unchanged. Resolve together with FR-P-031 and FR-P-032.
change_in: doc 50 §4; doc 52 §5.1-§5.4; D045; agent-runtime §13

title: The fixed 10-second stall card would fire on nearly every call of slow local setups
description: UX2 shows a stall card on any interactive wait longer than 10 s, offering 'use the default now', 'try the next route' and 'keep waiting'. On the reference 8 GB GPU with MoE offload, measured local calls take 6-25 s at warm p50, and CPU-only tiny models during Preview are slower still. (The default 4B session model's Picks are faster, and creative text on local runs is L4 background work, where UX2 does not apply.) For users of the offload path or CPU models the card becomes the normal state of every step instead of a signal. In a long run under Confirm the card repeats for each step. Doc 52 itself notes that if each switch needs a click, 'a busy host produces a stall card every time'. UX2 and §5.4 were doc 52 proposals when swept; D050 items 1 and 7 (2026-09-28) adopt them as the standard for rate-limited operation on cloud setups. Doc 38 §4.6's soft deadline applies to every model step.
evidence: doc 52 §4 (UX2, UX3, UX6, UX8), §5.4 (stall card), §6.1 (RG1 note); doc 49 via docs/README §5.6 ('Offload reaches whole-record Fill pass^3 0.917 at 6-25 s per call (warm p50)'); doc 53 latency classes (L3 <= 10 s) as cited in doc 52 §4; doc 38 §4.6.
frequency: constant: every step for users of offloaded or CPU-only local models
removal: Choose a safe default and explain at the point of friction. Set the threshold from the bound setup's own measured p90 latency for that step kind, which the ledger already records, but keep it bounded by the step's latency class, so a setup that is too slow for an L1 step shows as a fit problem at binding time instead of being hidden by a longer timeout. Below that threshold, show a progress bar with an ETA, not a card. Raise a card only for real anomalies: limit refusals, host errors, or p90 exceeded. Give every stall card 'apply to the rest of this run', so a long run asks once; a standing 'try the next route' is a reroute, which D050 item 3 allows along the user's route list, and each switch is still recorded, and a standing 'use the default now' leaves every kept default counted and chipped (UX6, UX8). Background steps never show a stall card. D050 item 1 now fixes UX2's 10-s card for limit-induced waits on cloud setups; applying a measured threshold to slow local setups, which D050's scope does not name, needs an owner note on D050. Resolve together with FR-M-008 and FR-P-032.
change_in: doc 52 §4 (UX2), §5.4; D024 (autonomy governs the stall card); D023 decision 3 (RG1); agent-runtime §12

title: Long runs stop for the user at moments nobody announced
description: With the default check-ins (premise, outline, end), a campaign run parks at S1 within minutes and again at S3, and its cards never time out. A user who starts a run and walks away comes back to find it has been waiting since the first minute. The plan card offers the check-ins choice but does not forecast when the run will need the user. OS notifications are opt-in, and nothing offers them at the moment they would matter.
evidence: D024 item 2 (Confirm default check-ins: premise, outline, end) and item 3; agent-runtime §10 (S1 premise ask, S3 approve); doc 38 §4.1 ('a card never times out into a yes'), §5.3 ('OS notifications while unfocused are opt-in'); doc 52 UX5 (the plan card says how long the run will take).
frequency: workflow: campaign runs
removal: Explain at the point of friction. The plan card shows a stop timeline computed from the plan: 'stops for you: premise at about 1 min, outline at about 6 min, then runs about 40 min on its own' (line 3 of the three-line card in FR-P-061). The check-ins choice and a one-click 'notify me' for this run sit beside the timeline. Questions that do not depend on model output, such as constraints for the premise, are asked before the run starts; S1's premise pick, which depends on model output, stays in the run.

title: 'Highlighted until seen' and the export warning for unreviewed text do not scale to a generated campaign
description: AI-made elements stay highlighted until the user has seen them, and exports warn about unreviewed model text. A campaign run creates hundreds of units, triggers, markers and lines across 8 or more missions. The map then shows highlights everywhere and the export warning fires on everything. The design has no bulk review, and 'seen' is not defined: in the viewport, selected, or opened in the inspector?
evidence: ui-shell §7 ('AI-made elements stay highlighted until the user has seen them ('new since you looked' is view state)'); doc 25 §9.1 ('an AI content report and an export warning for unreviewed model text'); agent-runtime §10 (S6 builds every node).
frequency: workflow: campaign and large mission runs
removal: Choose a safe default and eliminate steps. A review queue groups new elements by mission and kind, built from the provenance already stored, with 'mark reviewed' per group; 'mark reviewed' stays view state, as ui-shell §7 requires. Highlights clear on review or when the element's inspector is opened. The export warning states the count and links to the queue instead of listing items. Per-element provenance does not change.
change_in: ui-shell §7; doc 25 §9.1; core-document-model (view state only)

title: The decision inspector puts the whole decision record on one card
description: For each generated element, the inspector shows the capsule as sent, the menu, seed and pick, the model's 'why', checks and repairs, lens and pack versions, setup and cost, dependents, and the rules that did not run. Doc 63 adds the level, the knowledge pushed and the tools pulled. The everyday question is 'why is this here, and how do I change it?', and harness internals bury the answer. No layout is specified yet, so this is a design risk.

removal: Explain at the point of friction with layered disclosure; nothing is removed: (1) one code-written 'why' sentence, an origin chip (you, Wilco step, template, plugin), the validation status, and Edit, Pin and Re-roll; (2) the decision record: menu, pick, checks, repairs, dependents; (3) the capsule, seeds, versions and cost. The content is the same, and D010's full record stays one click away.

title: Defaults and template text look like finished content on the map and in Plotline
description: When a decision fails or is skipped, the code default stays in place, marked Defaulted, and the run summary says 'not done, default kept'. The inspector's value-source badges (ui-shell §5) already say 'engine default' or 'from template Ambush-2', but the natural views have no marker. A campaign with a dozen template briefings or default missions therefore looks complete: users can ship template text without noticing, or have to reread the run report to find it. The no-model path produces template text everywhere, so this also hits users with AI off.
evidence: doc 25 §10.1 ('marked Defaulted with the reason'), §10.2 step 6; doc 38 §5.3 (TurnReport: 'which defaults remain'); ui-shell §5 (value-source badges), §6 (defaulted appears only as run-panel counts); agent-runtime §10 (draft-first invariant); doc 52 UX6, UX8.

removal: Explain at the point of friction by extending an existing mechanism: reuse the inspector's value-source badges (ui-shell §5: 'engine default', 'from template Ambush-2', 'set by Wilco turn 12') as the single source for a chip, and surface them in the natural views (the map, the Plotline card via NodeSummary, the screenplay line) instead of adding a parallel marker. Add an advisory group in Problems and readiness ('12 lines still template text') with a one-click, priced 'fill these'. It is advice, never an error (D011), and never blocks export.

title: Stopped runs are labelled with their internal state, not with what the user must do next
description: A run can be Planned, Parked, Paused, BudgetLimited, QuotaLimited, Interrupted or Stopped, or have Stale steps, and each needs a different action from the user. How an interrupted run is offered after a crash or restart has no UI design; DG010 covers only the replay wording. When a catalog changes, a resumed run parks behind a three-way question ('re-run 3 steps / keep them / stop'), even though keeping the values and marking them stale is the non-destructive choice.
evidence: agent-runtime §5 (RunState and the staleness bullet); doc 38 §4.1, §4.2 (pure verify steps recomputed on resume), §4.3 step 3; doc 52 §6.1 (QuotaLimited); D025, open part DG010; doc 21 §6.5 ('a stale value is not called valid until re-checked'); doc 25 §9.2 ('nothing re-runs silently').
frequency: workflow: long runs, restarts, mod-set changes
removal: Choose a safe default and explain at the point of friction. One status chip states the next action: 'Waiting for you: pick a premise'; 'Out of budget: continue with 20 more turns, about $0.04'; 'Waiting for the quota reset at 00:00 UTC'; 'Interrupted: resume'. When a project opens, one non-modal card per interrupted run shows the settled answers that will be reused, the calls remaining and the cost. A digest mismatch keeps the settled values and marks them Stale with a reason chip; the dependent pure verify steps (recomputed on resume, doc 38 §4.2) re-check them against the current facts, only values that still pass continue, and those that fail park or re-run with a reason chip. 'Re-run 3 stale steps' is offered without blocking; nothing re-runs silently.
change_in: agent-runtime §5; doc 38 §4.1, §4.3; DG010

title: Five history actions, and 'rewind' means two different things
description: The user has to choose among ordinary undo; the History panel's rewind or replay; 'Rewind the run to here', which forks the journal; 'Revert this run', which undoes its groups where they commute; 'Re-run this step'; plus 'Compact AI history'. Rewind in the History panel moves the document; 'Rewind the run' forks a journal. Choosing the wrong one either loses later edits or does nothing visible. 'Replay' in the History panel also collides with DG010's reserved meaning of replay.
evidence: doc 38 §5.3 ('Three undo-like actions'); agent-runtime §5 ('Run lifecycle actions'; 'Compact AI history'); ui-shell §6 History row ('rewind or replay'); DG010 (replay).
frequency: workflow: every run the user wants to take back
removal: Make wrong input impossible. Each run appears as a collapsible group in the one History panel. 'Revert this run' is undo of that range, with the commute check. The journal fork is renamed 'Branch the run from here' and offered only from the run panel. The History panel's 'replay' gets a name that does not collide with DG010. Every action previews what it will change before applying. Human-origin groups stay untouched.
change_in: doc 38 §5.3; ui-shell §6; commands-undo-history §8; DG010

title: Idea card, Build it, plan card, Run takes two clicks for one decision
description: Idea cards are pitches. 'Build it' runs Dispatch and opens the workflow's plan card, which then needs Run. The first click already expresses the decision.
evidence: doc 21 §5.1 ('One that implies an edit carries a draft WorkflowCall; Build it runs Dispatch and the full workflow'); doc 38 §5.2; D024 (Auto never applies idea cards).
frequency: workflow: every idea card built
removal: Eliminate the step. The idea card carries a typed draft WorkflowCall, so code can compute the plan summary with no model call; the model-written arguments must still pass admission before the summary shows. The idea card then expands into its plan summary (the three-line card of FR-P-061) with Run on the card itself, so it takes one click when there is no warning to show. A click still carries UserIntent, and ideas are still never applied without one (Auto never applies them).
change_in: doc 21 §5.1; doc 38 §5.2; plotroom-wilco

title: Harness jargon and the persona's voice leak into user-facing AI surfaces
description: Internal terms reach the user in several places: the plan card and run panel show K and R, 'setups', admitted, defaulted and repaired counts, and 'continue with N more turns'; the inspector shows capsule, lens, digest and seed; badges say 'spike-checked' in one document and 'smoke-checked' in another, plus 'unqualified' and 'custom'; doc 63 adds 'asked as' levels and a grid of levels and badges. Question cards may be phrased in the signals-officer persona ('Insufficient intel: which town?'). Standing Orders has entries only for editor and engine concepts, so 'What is this?' has nothing to open on the AI surfaces.

removal: Rename, then explain at the point of friction. A code-owned map from each harness term to a user label (K: 'tries per choice', R: 'fix attempts', turns: calls and cost), with each label cleared in the names table. Internal ids appear only in the inspector's detail level, which keeps the glass box. Add Standing Orders entries for autonomy, effort, the plan card, pinned, stale, 'default kept' and each badge, reachable with 'What is this?'. Computed questions, findings and errors are always in plain voice; the persona speaks only in the flavour slot (a design edit to doc 21 §11.7). Resolve together with FR-P-026 and FR-C-009.

title: Core UI words have several meanings: Ask, preset, router, badge, mode, rewind, draft
description: 'Ask' is an autonomy level, a chat mode, a step kind, the menu escape Q, and Dispatch::Ask. 'Preset' covers effort presets, per-model harness presets, 'connect a free model' presets, the Easy/Advanced view preset, difficulty presets, composition, attribute, module and settings presets, component presets, event-pacing presets and MP slot presets. 'Router' is a Wilco role, the quota-aware router, and a campaign decision node. 'Badge' covers fit, qualification, Requires, value-source, NeedsInput and external-agent badges. 'Mode' covers F1-F6, chat, Explain, Teach, Tutor, Economy, offline, expert, safe and accessibility modes. Users read one word and form the wrong mental model. Models asked about 'presets' or 'ask' must work out which one is meant. Contributors choose names inconsistently.

For example: autonomy levels become Read-only / Suggest / Confirm / Auto; the router role becomes 'dispatcher' (acceptable only if the role really performs IntentFill and Dispatch, since the name sits close to the internal Dispatch type; check it in the names table); harness presets become 'model tuning'; and 'preset' is kept for a single user-level concept. Renames go through D034's names table and the doc 02 §9 clearance. Resolve in one names-table pass with FR-P-035, FR-P-052 and FR-C-009.

'The Tote' (from 'tote board') means nothing to most users. Teller is mostly hidden behind diagnostics, so its name adds vocabulary with little payoff. D002 says the generic terms stay valid in prose, but nothing requires the UI to show them next to the names.

The palette and search match the plain words. The names table requires a descriptor for every name. No rename is needed. Showing 'script check' in place of Teller would reverse D002 and D034 item 2, so it is an owner question through the names table, not part of this removal. Resolve together with FR-P-002.

description: Different documents give similar buttons different behaviour. 'Surprise me' is code-only dice in doc 43: $0, instant, offline. In doc 21 §6.3, 'surprise me' pitches are a Required model workflow. Doc 41's 'surprise me' makes seeded atmosphere variants. Doc 25 has Twist and Reroll; doc 43 adds Roll 10, four remix levels, the Seed Atlas, campaign modifiers, event pacing and a play-seed policy. Doc 43 suggests hiding the extras in the Easy view, but D029 makes Advanced the default, so newcomers see every knob.

title: Nothing teaches a newcomer what Wilco can do, or that most generators work without it
area: wilco-ux: learning what AI can do
description: Wilco is off by default, with no provider configured. Drill's curriculum (tracks A-C) teaches editor and engine concepts, with no lesson on Wilco, plan cards, undoing AI edits, inspecting or pinning. Doc 33 never mentions Wilco, and the only onboarding is one dismissible welcome card that offers Drill. The AI-off workflows (templates, give-patrol, validate-and-fix, campaign from brief with template text) are easy to mistake for AI features that need setup. Nothing answers 'what can Wilco do here?' for the current selection.
evidence: D004 (Wilco off by default); agent-runtime §1 (Default state); doc 33 §4.8 ('No start-up tour; at most one dismissible welcome card offers Drill') and §5.4 (curriculum); doc 33 has no mention of Wilco; doc 21 §6.3 (Forbidden and Optional workflows run with AI off); doc 38 §5.1 (palette entries greyed with a one-click fix); D028.

A Drill lesson, 'Working with Wilco', runs on the $0 template path with no provider and teaches run, inspect, edit, pin, re-roll and undo; its steps stay validator-checked by code, and adding it changes D028's curriculum (a design-round item). The welcome card offers both.

title: External agents start runs blind: they poll, cannot see what is waiting, and each direct edit gets its own card
description: A run started over MCP waits in Planned for a click in the editor, and its ask and approve cards can be answered only in the editor. The agent must poll workflow.status and cannot tell its user what to click, so it keeps polling, spends calls and tokens, may trip the server's per-session repetition limits, or retries workflow.start and creates duplicate runs. Direct command proposals from MCP always wait for confirmation, whatever the autonomy. The MCP tools are generated one per registry command, so an agent making 20 edits leaves 20 pending cards and 20 round trips, and a partially accepted set leaves half a change in the mission. workflow.list does not say which workflows will stop for the human mid-run, so the agent cannot pick one that will finish. The human gate is an invariant, so the friction cannot be removed, only explained and made cheap. Merged from two duplicate model-facing findings (one card per proposed command; runs waiting for the user look like runs working).
evidence: doc 38 §9 (approvals stay in the editor; 'polling workflow.status works meanwhile'; the primer should prefer workflow.start; MCP Tasks support unknown), AT-W15; extensibility §10 ('external direct command proposals always wait for confirmation regardless of the autonomy setting'; tools generated from the command registry), §12 OQ4; agent-runtime §2 (ProposeOp carries batches), §15; commands-undo-history §3, §4.1 (plan and admit on a Scratch fork), §4.4 (UserIntent); doc 61 §4.7 (draft on a Scratch fork with one final admission); doc 56 PK3 (per-session call and repetition limits); D036 item 6. Measure: polling calls per run, and one pending card per direct edit.
frequency: constant: every external-agent run and every multi-edit request
removal: Explain at the point of friction, and eliminate calls. (a) workflow.start and workflow.status return a read-only typed 'awaiting' field (kind: plan approval, ask card, approve card or quota reset; the card id and title, the question text, the time it started waiting, and the next action in words) that the agent can relay to its user. (b) workflow.status takes a bounded wait-for-change parameter (long-poll) instead of requiring busy polling, with MCP progress notifications where the client supports them. (c) workflow.start is idempotent by a client key, so a retry never creates a second run. (d) One batch-proposal tool, changeset.propose, takes a list of typed commands, plans them on a Scratch fork, admits them as one batch, shows one card with a semantic diff and applies them as one undo group. (e) workflow.list states how many user stops each workflow has under the current autonomy. (f) The editor badges waiting external cards. Consent still requires UserIntent in the editor, and nothing auto-applies (extensibility §12 OQ4 stays 'never'). Resolve together with FR-M-002.
change_in: doc 38 §9; extensibility §10; agent-runtime §15; commands-undo-history §4.4; plotroom-mcp

title: What waits for a click is specified in seven places, and they disagree
description: The rules for waits come from seven places: D024, doc 21 §7.3, doc 38 §5.4, doc 52 §5.4 (stall cards per autonomy level), extensibility §10 (external proposals always wait), D043 (the egress card every time for derived sends) and commands-undo-history §4.4 (UserIntent). Doc 63 §7 adds reliance on the size threshold. Doc 21 §4.2 and doc 38 §5.2 already disagree on whether a small requested edit shows a plan card. An implementer or coding agent will hard-code one reading at each call site, and users will then see inconsistent behaviour.
evidence: the sections cited above; D024 Consequences (the only enforcement is the lint on effort predicates); agent-runtime §11 (the dials table states waits only in prose).
frequency: workflow: every wait decision in code
removal: Make wrong input impossible. One table in agent-runtime §11 maps wait kind x autonomy x origin to wait or no wait, with the reason. One pure function with exhaustive matches implements it, for example wait_for(WaitKind, Autonomy, Origin) -> Wait, with a table-driven test over every cell, which keeps autonomy as the only dial (D024) and makes safety waits unskippable by construction. The other documents point to the table instead of restating it. The plan-card receipt rule (FR-P-060), the size threshold (FR-P-062) and the controls simplification (FR-P-063) land as rows of this table. Resolve together with FR-P-033.
change_in: agent-runtime §11; D024 (consequence note); plotroom-workflow-runtime
effort: S for the doc; S for the code later

title: The names table that D034 relies on does not exist yet
description: D034 delegates every pending user-facing name to one names table that the owner reviews before release, and D028 requires each new name to clear the doc 02 §9 checklist before its UI string is written. No table exists yet, and the roadmap schedules it for M4. Placeholder names are scattered across research docs: Economy mode, Surprise me, Seed Atlas, Remix, Event pacing, Thin roster, the Director names of DG037, and the realism levels. People writing research docs, and later coding agents writing UI strings, have no single place to check a name or its collisions, so collisions keep accumulating.

removal: Eliminate the step. Create the table now, as data: name, plain descriptor, status (placeholder or cleared), clearance date, collisions, owner review. Route every new name through it. Once UI code exists, a UI-string lint checks that every user-visible term is in the table. This is the precondition for FR-P-076, FR-P-035, FR-P-052, FR-P-075, FR-P-077 and FR-P-005.
